transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-17
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Noah Patel (CTO - CobaltBridge), Maya Chen (Principal ML Eng - CobaltBridge), Elliot Gardner (Infra Lead - CobaltBridge)
Artifacts mentioned: shared sheet (drive.google.com/.../cobaltbridge-workload), redwood benchmark template (link), security questionnaire (link)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, I'm Jordan from Redwood, and with me is Priya our solutions engineer. quick round robin?
[00:06] Noah: hi, Noah here, CTO at CobaltBridge. we're building a customer support summarization+action routing product, expecting a lot of short requests but occasional long threads.
[00:12] Maya: Maya — I own the model infra and the telemetry we can share.
[00:15] Elliot: Elliot, infra lead, network and k8s, will own any VPC/on-prem constraints.
[00:20] Jordan: great. goal today is to scope a POC that validates cost and latency at your observed peak shapes. specifically we want QPS, concurrency quantiles, token mix, and then design a benchmark matrix.

[00:36] Priya: quick question, when you say "lots of short requests and occasional long threads" — can you ballpark average input token length and the long-tail frequency?
[00:44] Noah: median input is about 50–70 tokens, but 5% of requests are long, like 800 to 2,000 input tokens because it's multi-email threads. outputs vary; most responses are 60–120 tokens but generated action plans can be 600 tokens sometimes.
[01:02] Maya: to add, in the last month our 95th percentile output was around 780 tokens, p99 about 1,400 but that's partly because we have some flows that dump whole threads into the model.

[01:22] Priya: ah okay — that's helpful. for capacity planning we typically ask for three quantiles: median, 95th, and 99th token counts for input and output. do you have token histograms or a sample export?
[01:32] Maya: we can provide a token-level export, we haven't normalized emojis and attachments so counts are a bit noisy. we'll clean and upload.

[01:42] Jordan: perfect. on QPS/concurrency, what does your traffic look like over an hour/day? bursty or steady?
[01:48] Noah: mostly steady during business hours, but blunt spikes during large incident escalations. typical steady QPS is 10–15 qps, peak sustained bursts hit 120 qps for 4–6 minutes, and we see concurrent requests spike to 45–60 in those windows.
[02:04] Elliot: our app frontend does some batching but it's not consistent — sometimes clients send single messages which increases concurrency.

[02:16] Priya: ok so peak QPS 120 and peak concurrency 60 for short windows. that's a helpful starting point. one immediate question: do you need guaranteed p95 latency under a given number or is cost more important?
[02:28] Noah: we have two priorities: user-facing p95 below 300ms for short responses, for long generation flows we can accept up to 1.5s p95. cost target is to keep inference cost per 1k tokens under $0.80 if possible.
[02:40] Jordan: noted — we'll design benchmarks for both short and long flows and include cost-per-1k simulation.

[02:50] Priya: for the benchmark matrix, suggested axes: model variant (open-llama / redwood-tuned / quantized), GPU profile (A10G x1, A10G x4, A100x8), batching configs (no batching, 50ms batching, 200ms batching), and workload slices (median short, 95th mix, long-tail heavy).
[03:12] Maya: can you quantify the effect of batching on tail latency? in our infra we worry about adding latency to short requests.
[03:18] Priya: yes, batching helps throughput and reduces cost per token but you pay batching delay. for low-latency short requests we'll recommend small batching windows (10–50ms) and prefix KV caching for repeated context; for long outputs batching can be larger. we'll include both.

[03:38] Jordan: also want to flag model fallbacks — if a large model is busy we can fall back to a quantized variant or smaller model to keep p95 within acceptable bound.
[03:48] Noah: how seamless is fallback? we must preserve deterministic routing for audit.
[03:53] Priya: routing is policy based and we record fallback events in audit logs. there's a slight diff in output quality but we'll capture this in the evals and include rollback triggers.

[04:06] Elliot: networking question — in the VPC case what's the expected egress pattern? we want to know if sustained 120 qps to an external endpoint will require special network config.
[04:16] Jordan: for Redwood Private we can do customer-controlled egress inside the VPC; for Hosted customers traffic leaves our infra to the model pool but we support peering and direct routing. we'll send the VPC checklist.

[04:28] Priya: back to workload telemetry — Maya, if you can export a 2-week sliding window with timestamps, request IDs, input_tokens, output_tokens, and response time, we'll reconstruct concurrency and QPS distributions. the shared spreadsheet has a template.
[04:42] Maya: yes, we'll map fields. note some timestamps are client local time, might need normalization.

[04:50] Priya: that's fine, we usually align on UTC. next, success criteria: propose the POC pass if both conditions met: 1) p95 latency for short-flow < 300ms at your 95th concurrency slice, and 2) end-to-end cost per 1k tokens below your $0.80 target on the recommended config. additionally, no functional regressions on a 10-case eval suite.
[05:16] Noah: sounds fair. can you also include p99 SLOs? we care about tail on incident flows, want p99 < 2s for short, < 4s for long flows.
[05:26] Jordan: yes we'll include p99 targets in the benchmark matrix.

[05:34] Priya: let's talk throughput shaping in the benchmark. we run two modes: steady-state (sustained 15 qps for 30 minutes) and burst tests (ramp to 120 qps for 6 minutes with concurrency up to 60). we'll measure token saturation, GPU utilization, and queuing.
[05:50] Elliot: for burst tests, we need to ensure our ingress LB doesn't silently queue; I can provision a test route to mimic prod.
[05:56] Jordan: perfect. Priya, can you note the telemetry we'll collect?
[06:00] Priya: sure — per-request latency, server-side queue wait, GPU utilization, tokens in/out, memory and KV cache hit rate, and per-instance logs for OOMs. we'll also capture cost model estimates based on the GPU-hours used and token counts.

[06:12] Maya: about tokenization — we use a custom tokenizer that sometimes counts attachments as multiple tokens; might skew the histogram. is that a big problem?
[06:20] Priya: we can normalize by running our tokenization pass on a sample of your payloads. if there's a mismatch we'll annotate the histograms and run the benchmark with both tokenization assumptions.

[06:30] Jordan: quick aside on KV cache: since you have repeated context for the same customer ID, we can set a prefix cache to reduce recomputation. expected win depends on reuse ratio — do you have reuse estimates?
[06:40] Maya: reuse is about 40% within a 5-minute window for active customers.
[06:45] Priya: that will give a noticeable reduction in tokens processed — we'll model both with and without KV cache.

[06:54] Noah: curious on hardware: what baseline do you recommend for the initial POC infra? we don't want to overcommit.
[07:00] Priya: for your mix (short-heavy but with long tails), recommended starting configs: 4x A10G for the main test (good cost-performance), and a heavier run on 8x A100 if you want to test worst-case tail and concurrent large outputs. we'll include a smaller 1x A10 run for baseline latency.
[07:16] Jordan: also will provide an estimate of cost per 1k tokens for each config in the spreadsheet.

[07:24] Elliot: will Redwood provide automation for running the benchmark (replay harness)?
[07:28] Priya: yes, we'll share a harness that replays request traces at desired QPS and token length distributions. it will emit metrics in prometheus and an S3/drive output of raw traces.

[07:36] Maya: on evaluation, we want a small human-judged quality check for fallback cases to ensure outputs are acceptable.
[07:42] Jordan: we'll include a 10-case blind eval and a quality rubric. if fallback quality drops below threshold we'll mark as fail.

[07:50] Noah: timeline question — how quickly can we run the initial POC? we have some compliance gating but can give infra access in about two weeks.
[07:58] Jordan: assuming telemetry uploaded in 3–5 days and infra access in two weeks, Priya estimates 2 weeks for benchmark runs and analysis, so total ~5 weeks to POC report.
[08:08] Priya: rough timeline: day 0 collect telemetry, day 3 finalize matrix, week 1 run baseline and medium, week 2 run burst and heavy tail, then 3–4 days for analysis and report.

[08:22] Elliot: security: we'll need SOC2 docs and notes on encryption, KMS options if using Private.
[08:28] Jordan: we'll attach SOC2 summary and the security questionnaire. Private has KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs for fallbacks.

[08:36] Maya: small note: in our logs we also see rare akka-timeout artifacts, so some p99s might be client-side. will you help parse that out?
[08:44] Priya: yes, the harness will capture client and server timestamps so we can distinguish client-side timeout vs server queuing.

[08:52] Jordan: do we have any other constraints?
[08:55] Noah: only that we can't expose PII in any logs; we'll scrub or token-id hash before sharing.
[09:01] Priya: understoood — share hashed ids.

[09:06] Jordan: recap of next steps: Jordan to share workload spreadsheet and benchmark template; Maya to upload telemetry; Elliot to confirm networking constraints; Priya to run the initial benchmark sweep when infra is ready; schedule follow-up to review results.
[09:18] Noah: happy with that, thanks all.
[09:22] Jordan: thanks, meeting adjourned.

Notes on fuzzy transcription and artifacts: some technical terms mis-transcribed (e.g., "KV cache" as "K-V cash", "A100" heard as "A-one-hundred"), occasional overlapping talk at 07:24-07:36, timestamps approximate.

Benchmark matrix highlights (to be filled in spreadsheet):
- Short-flow slice: input median 60 tokens, output median 90 tokens, target p95 < 300ms, p99 < 2s.
- Long-flow slice: input median 900 tokens (95th 1,800), output median 600 tokens, target p95 < 1.5s, p99 < 4s.
- Peak shape: burst to 120 qps, concurrency up to 60 for 4–6 minutes (stress test).
- Hardware to test: 1x A10G, 4x A10G, 8x A100.
- Batching/windowing: 0ms (no batching), 10/50/200ms windows.
- Cache configs: KV cache enabled vs disabled.
- Eval: blind 10-case quality check, fallback acceptance threshold 0.8 agreement with baseline.

End of transcript.
